title: Two Hours in Abu Dhabi, and Modi Walked Away With $5 Billion and a Defence Pact That Rewrites India-UAE Ties
excerpt: The whirlwind visit yielded six agreements spanning defence, energy, AI, and maritime security — a strategic recalibration driven by the Iran war and Gulf realignment
body:
When Narendra Modi touched down in Abu Dhabi on May 15 for what was officially described as a two-hour stopover en route to Europe, few expected the visit to produce the kind of strategic haul that typically takes months of diplomatic groundwork. Yet by the time his aircraft was wheels-up again, India and the United Arab Emirates had signed six agreements, unlocked $5 billion in fresh investment commitments, and established a defence partnership framework that neither side had previously been willing to formalise.

The centrepiece is a strategic defence cooperation pact — the first of its kind between the two nations. It covers joint military production, maritime security, cyber defence, and advanced technology sharing. For India, which has spent decades calibrating its Gulf relationships to avoid taking sides, this is a significant step. For the UAE, which exited OPEC last year and has been quietly distancing itself from the Saudi-led bloc, it represents a hedge against regional isolation as the Iran conflict continues to simmer.

## The Energy Architecture

The energy component alone would have justified the visit. ADNOC, the UAE's state oil company, agreed to expand its strategic petroleum reserve storage in India by 30 million barrels — a move that effectively turns Indian salt caverns into an extension of Emirati energy infrastructure. A separate $2.5 billion liquefied natural gas deal with ADNOC Gas will see India receive 500,000 tonnes of LNG annually for the next decade, making it ADNOC's single largest customer.

The LPG supply agreement is equally consequential. The UAE already provides roughly 40 per cent of India's cooking gas needs. The new memorandum of understanding formalises a long-term supply corridor at a time when India is grappling with a ₹3-per-litre fuel price hike that has triggered inflation fears and gig-worker strikes at home.

For the 3.5 million Indians living in the Gulf — the largest expatriate community in the UAE — these deals are not abstractions. Energy security means stable fuel prices at home, which in turn means stable household budgets for families that depend on remittances. Defence cooperation means a more predictable security environment in a region where the Strait of Hormuz remains the world's most consequential chokepoint.

## The Investment Equation

The $5 billion investment package is split across several vehicles. The UAE's sovereign wealth apparatus approved a $3 billion acquisition stake in RBL Bank, signalling a deepening appetite for Indian financial services. Another $1 billion is earmarked for Sammaan Capital. The remaining commitments flow into infrastructure, AI supercomputing capacity, and a ship repair cluster that will be developed jointly.

The AI component is particularly notable. The two sides agreed to collaborate on supercomputing infrastructure, a move that aligns with India's ambition to build domestic AI capacity rather than relying entirely on American hyperscalers. For the UAE, which has invested heavily in AI through its national strategy, India offers scale — both in data and in engineering talent.

## Why Now?

The timing is not coincidental. The Iran-UAE tensions that have been building since the Iran war escalated in early 2026 have reshaped Gulf security calculations. The UAE's exit from OPEC was itself a signal of strategic autonomy, and its willingness to sign a defence pact with India — rather than relying exclusively on the traditional American security umbrella — suggests a broader diversification of strategic partnerships.

India, meanwhile, needs energy stability ahead of what promises to be a difficult monsoon season and a domestic economy adjusting to higher fuel costs. Locking in long-term LNG and LPG supply at predictable terms is as much macroeconomic prudence as it is diplomatic strategy.

Modi's five-nation tour continues through Europe, where trade negotiations with the Netherlands and others are on the agenda. But the Abu Dhabi stop may prove to be the most consequential leg of the journey — a reminder that in the current geopolitical environment, two hours with the right counterpart can yield more than two years of multilateral summitry.

The question for India's Gulf diaspora is whether the institutional architecture being built around these agreements can deliver on its promise. Defence pacts and energy MoUs are only as good as their implementation. For now, though, the trajectory is unmistakable: India and the UAE are no longer just trading partners. They are becoming strategic allies.
